name: Urapmin
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Only anthropological literature (Robbins) surfaced; no linguistic description of stress located

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is predictable by the following rules: Primary stress occurs on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel. In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is closed by a consonant, primary stress occurs on the final syllable. In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is open, primary stress occurs on the initial syllable. The above rules apply to the stems of inflected words.
new_statements.citation: Steinkraus, Walter. 1969. Tifal phonology showing vowel and tone neutralization. Kivung 2(1): 57-66.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. is a 10-page ScanSnap scan with no text (extracted text empty). I rendered p. 8 (printed p. 64) and read the page scan: heading '7. Stress' and the four sentences quoted in the report are there word for word ('Primary stress is predictable by the following rules: / Primary stress occurs on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel. / In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is closed by a consonant, primary stress occurs on the final syllable. / In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is open, primary stress occurs on…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable, not contrastive. The first long-vowel syllable of the word takes primary stress; if every vowel is short, stress goes to the final syllable when it is closed (CVC) and to the initial syllable when the final syllable is open. Inflected words stress their stem by the same rules (Boush 1994: on the final syllable of a simple verb stem). Vowel length is the weight criterion; coda weight only decides the all-short case.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress occurs on the second syllable with a lengthened vowel. In inflected words with more than three syllables in which all vowels are short, secondary stress occurs on the antepenult. No secondary stress occurs in words of three or less syllables in which all vowels are short.' (p. 64)
new_statements.exceptions: Non-inflected words of more than three syllables with all short vowels: 'extremely rare, and stress rules have not yet been posited for them.' No secondary stress in all-short words of three or fewer syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: rules are stated for non-inflected words of two or three syllables and for the stems of inflected words; longer uninflected all-short words 'extremely rare, and stress rules have not yet been posited for them'. Tifal also has two tonemes (high/low, one per syllable, §6 p. 63-64), so stress is a predictable, non-contrastive prominence alongside lexical tone. Steinkraus's data are from Tifalmin proper (Okbilabip, Ilam valley; fn. 1), not from Urapmin villages. The Boush 1994 Tifal OPD (p. 3), which explicitly lists Urapmin as a Tifal village, gives the same rule in short form and adds 'On inflected words primary stress occurs on the final syllable of a simple verb stem.' Contrast: Healey 1964 ch. IV §7.3 found no consistent loudness differences in Telefol, the language on Urapmin's other side.
new_statements.identity_note: No source describes Urapmin as such. The quoted statement is for Tifal [tif] (Glottolog tifa1245), Tifalmin dialect (Okbilabip). Healey 1964: 40-41 treats the Urapmin as a Tifal-speaking clan forming the 'Tifalmin-Urapmin' dialect group of Tifal, and the Boush 1994 Tifal OPD lists Urapmin among the Tifal 'major villages' and cites Urapmin-specific segmental features (initial /l/, /kw/) while giving the same stress rule; Wikipedia likewise lists Urap(min) as a Tifal dialect. Ethnologue/ISO separated Urapmin [urm] as 'geographically and linguistically between Tifal [tif] and Telefol [tlf]'. Telefol (tele1256; Healey 1964 ch. IV §7.3) is reported to have no detectable stress, so the Tifal rule should be filed for Urapmin only as a dialect-group proxy, flagged as such.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is predictable on non-inflected words by the following rules: -primary stress occurs on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel. [...] -in non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all the vowels are short and in which the final syllable is closed by a consonant, primary stress occurs on the final syllable. [...] -in non-inflected words [...] in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is open, primary stress occurs on the initial syllable. [...] -primary stress on inflected words occur on the final syllable of a simple verb stem. Secondary stress occurs on inflected words of four or more syllables, and then, on the final syllable suffix.
new_statements.citation: Boush, Al & Susan Boush. 1974 (April). Tifal phonology. Ukarumpa: SIL ms., 43 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives 31073.
new_statements.locator: §3.3.1 Stress, pp. 25-27 (pp. 28-30); fn. 3 p. 25 on tone; p. 30 on pitch-stress relation
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'Tifal phonology', Author 'Boush, Al and Susan Boush') and rendered pp. 28-30 (= ms pp. 25-27) at 150 dpi. p. 25: '3.3.1 Stress. Primary stress is predictable on non-inflected words by the following rules: -primary stress occurs on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel.' fn. 3: 'Thus far, tone has been found to be non-contrastive. This differs from the work done in a related dialect by Walter Steinkraus, TIFAL TONE. Stress seems to be more crucial.' p. 26: the closed-final -> final-stress rule, the open-final -> initial-stress rule, and '-primary stress on inflected words occur on the final syllable of a simple verb stem. Secondary stress occu…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement rules, almost verbatim, as the existing Steinkraus 1969 statement (first long vowel; else final closed / initial open), so it agrees; it adds the inflected-verb rule (final syllable of a simple stem), a secondary-stress rule, and the claim that tone is non-contrastive in this dialect (Balemtilabib, Lam River valley, p. 1), whereas Steinkraus's dialect has two tones. The work is about Tifal; it never mentions Urapmin.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress goes to the first long (geminate) vowel; if all vowels are short, a 2-3-syllable uninflected word is stressed on the final syllable when that syllable is closed and on the initial syllable when it is open; in inflected verbs primary stress falls on the final syllable of a simple verb stem. Footnote 3 (p. 25): 'Thus far, tone has been found to be non-contrastive. This differs from the work done in a related dialect by Walter Steinkraus, TIFAL TONE. Stress seems to be more crucial.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 26: 'Secondary stress occurs on inflected words of four or more syllables, and then, on the final syllable suffix.' Examples p. 27 (e.g. /dolnokomab/ ['dolnogo,map] 'you will write').
new_statements.exceptions: p. 27: 'stress rules for complex or compound verbs have not been posited at this time.' p. 30: 'Further research needs to be done in intonational patterns, especially in its relation to primary stress. The inter relationship between the two is not fully clear although there is a tendency for pitch and primary stress to frequently co-occur.'
new_statements.identity_note: No work opened describes Urapmin. Boush & Boush 1974 is Tifal as spoken at Balemtilabib in the Lam River valley (p. 1); Steinkraus 1969 (existing statement) is 'a related dialect' of Tifal; Healey 1964 PL B-3 is Telefol of the Kayalikmin parish, Ifitaman valley (p. 2). Urapmin is placed between Tifal and Telefol (Ethnologue; Healey's thesis treats the Urapmin as a Tifal-speaking clan, per the existing note), so the weight-sensitive reading is a Tifal proxy, and the nearest Telefol description says there is no word stress at all.

readall_conflicts: The two Tifal sources agree on stress placement (Boush & Boush 1974 repeats Steinkraus 1969's rules: first long vowel, else final closed syllable, else initial) but disagree on tone: Steinkraus 1969 posits two tonemes for his Tifal dialect, while Boush & Boush 1974 (Balemtilabib, Lam River valley) say tone is non-contrastive in theirs and that stress is 'more crucial'. Healey 1964 (Telefol, PL B-3) is a different language of the Mountain Ok group and denies any consistent word stress, analysing the prosody as two tonemes; that is a difference in prosodic type from the Tifal statements, not a different stress placement. None of the three works describes Urapmin itself.
